paper.title: Weight regain and cardiometabolic effects after withdrawal of semaglutide: The STEP 1 trial extension.
paper.citation: Wilding et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2022

claims.finding: From week 0 to week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% (SD: 9.3%) with semaglutide and 2.0% (SD: 6.1%) with placebo; following treatment withdrawal, semaglutide and placebo participants regained 11.6 (SD: 7.7) and 1.9 (SD: 4.8) percentage points of lost weight, respectively, by week 120, resulting in net losses from week 0 to week 120 of 5.6% (SD: 8.9%) with semaglutide and 0.1% (SD: 5.8%) with placebo.
claims.quote: From week 0 to week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% (SD: 9.3%) with semaglutide and 2.0% (SD: 6.1%) with placebo. Following treatment withdrawal, semaglutide and placebo participants regained 11.6 (SD: 7.7) and 1.9 (SD: 4.8) percentage points of lost weight, respectively, by week 120, resulting in net losses of 5.6% (SD: 8.9%) and 0.1% (SD: 5.8%), respectively, from week 0 to week 120.

claims.finding: One year after stopping once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg and lifestyle intervention, participants regained two-thirds of their prior weight loss and experienced similar changes in cardiometabolic factors.
claims.quote: One year after withdrawal of once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg and lifestyle intervention, participants regained two-thirds of their prior weight loss, with similar changes in cardiometabolic variables.

claims.finding: In the semaglutide arm, participants with week 0 to week 68 weight losses of < 5%, ≥ 5%-< 10%, ≥ 10%-< 15%, ≥ 15%-< 20%, and ≥ 20% had net weight changes from week 0 to week 120 of 4.2% (SD: 6.2%), –0.7% (SD: 5.9%), –1.8% (SD: 5.0%), –5.5% (SD: 7.2%), and –12.1% (SD: 8.9%), respectively.
claims.quote: Participants in the semaglutide arm with weight losses (i.e. < 5%, ≥ 5%-< 10%, ≥ 10%-< 15%, ≥ 15%-< 20% and ≥ 20%) from week 0 to week 68 had net weight changes from week 0 to week 120 of 4.2% (SD: 6.2%), –0.7% (SD: 5.9%), –1.8% (SD: 5.0%), –5.5% (SD: 7.2%) and –12.1% (SD: 8.9%), respectively.

claims.finding: Among participants not using any obesity pharmacotherapy during the extension, mean weight changes from week 0 to week 120 were –5.6% (SD: 8.9%) in the semaglutide group and –0.3% (SD: 5.3%) in the placebo group.
claims.quote: Among the subgroup not using obesity pharmacotherapy, mean changes in body weight from week 0 to week 120 were –5.6% (SD: 8.9%) and –0.3% (SD: 5.3%) in the semaglutide and placebo arms, respectively.

claims.finding: Among participants with prediabetes at baseline, 93.6% reverted to normoglycaemia at week 68 with semaglutide compared with 41.5% with placebo.
claims.quote: Among participants with prediabetes at baseline, numerically more participants reverted to normoglycaemia at week 68 with semaglutide than placebo (93.6% vs. 41.5%; Figure 3).

claims.finding: At week 120, 43.3% of baseline prediabetes participants in the semaglutide arm maintained reversion to normoglycaemia compared to 34.0% in the placebo arm.
claims.quote: Although the deterioration was larger in the semaglutide arm, a relative improvement was maintained versus the placebo arm at week 120, with reversion to normoglycaemia in 43.3% versus 34.0% of participants with baseline prediabetes in the semaglutide and placebo arms, respectively.

claims.finding: The lifestyle intervention comprised counselling every 4 weeks regarding diet (a 500 kcal daily deficit relative to total estimated energy expenditure at randomization) and physical activity (150 minutes per week).
claims.quote: The lifestyle intervention consisted of counselling every 4 weeks on diet (500 kcal deficit per day relative to total estimated energy expenditure at randomization) and physical activity (150 minutes per week).

claims.finding: The main limitations of the extension study included its relatively small sample size compared to the main STEP 1 trial population and selecting trial sites based on highest main phase recruitment, which could cause selection bias.
claims.quote: The key limitations of the extension were the relatively small sample size compared with the main STEP 1 trial population and the selection of sites based on those with the highest recruitment in the STEP 1 main phase, which could introduce an element of selection bias.

claims.finding: All extension phase analyses were exploratory, and no formal statistical significance testing was conducted.
claims.quote: In addition, all analyses were exploratory and thus no formal tests of statistical significance were performed.

rejected.finding: At week 120 (52 weeks off-treatment), a weight loss of 5% or higher from baseline was observed in 48.2% of participants (95 of 197) in the semaglutide arm compared with 22.6% (21 of 93) in the placebo arm.
rejected.quote: At week 120, 5% or higher weight loss from baseline was observed in 48.2% of participants (95 of 197) in the semaglutide arm and in 22.6% (21 of 93) in the placebo arm.

rejected.finding: After treatment was stopped, mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased in both groups and returned to baseline levels by week 120.
rejected.quote: After treatment withdrawal, mean SBP and DBP increased in both treatment arms, reverting to baseline levels by week 120 (Figure 2 and Tables 2 and S1).

draft.message: When GLP-1 medicines stop without guidance, weight can return, which is why a doctor-led exit strategy and long-term habit support are essential.
draft.reasoning: Indian adults considering GLP-1 medicines often worry that any weight lost will return once treatment ends. This content addresses that exact concern using clinical trial data while explaining how Steer's doctor-led approach helps members build lasting habits and navigate a planned exit.

carousel.body: Here is what clinical trial research shows happens to body weight when treatment ends.

carousel.headline: In trial participants, stopping treatment led to weight regain.
carousel.body: One year after stopping once-weekly subcutaneous GLP-1 medicine 2.4 mg and lifestyle intervention, participants regained two-thirds of their prior weight loss.

carousel.headline: Mean weight loss changed over 120 weeks.
carousel.body: From week 0 to week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% with the medicine in this trial and 2.0% with placebo.

carousel.headline: Net weight loss decreased after treatment ended.

draft.caption:
Is weight regain inevitable after stopping weight loss medicine? Research shows that one year after stopping once-weekly subcutaneous GLP-1 medicine 2.4 mg and lifestyle intervention, participants regained two-thirds of their prior weight loss. From week 0 to week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% with the medicine, but after stopping, net loss dropped to 5.6% by week 120.

At Steer, we focus on doctor-led care, thorough screening, and long-term habit support. You need a long-term plan made with your doctor, including what happens when the medicine stops.

Before you start, hear it from a doctor, not a reel.
